text: NIKE, Inc. was incorporated in 1967 under the laws of the State of Oregon. The terms “we,” “us,” “NIKE,” and the “Company” refer to NIKE, Inc. and its predecessors, subsidiaries, and affiliates, collectively, unless the context indicates otherwise. The Company’s NIKE digital commerce website is located at www.nike.com, and its corporate website, investors.nike.com, posts filings such as the annual report on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, current reports on Form 8-K, and amendments to those reports as soon as reasonably practicable after they are electronically filed with or furnished to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”). Definitive Proxy Statements are also posted on the corporate website, and all such filings are available free of charge on the SEC’s website (www.sec.gov). Copies of corporate governance documents, including committee charters, corporate governance guidelines, and the code of ethics, are available on the corporate website and can be provided in print upon written request to NIKE Investor Relations at One Bowerman Drive, Beaverton, Oregon 97005-6453. The Company’s principal business activity involves the design, development, and worldwide marketing and sale of athletic footwear, apparel, equipment, accessories, and services. NIKE is the largest seller of athletic footwear and apparel globally. Products are sold through NIKE-owned retail stores and digital platforms (collectively referred to as “NIKE Direct”), to retail accounts, and to independent distributors, licensees, and sales representatives in virtually all countries. Virtually all products are manufactured by independent contractors; nearly all footwear and apparel are produced outside the United States, while equipment is produced both in the U.S. and abroad. The Company focuses its NIKE Brand offerings in six key categories: Running, NIKE Basketball, the Jordan Brand, Football (Soccer), Training, and Sportswear (sports-inspired lifestyle products), as well as products for kids and other athletic and recreational activities such as American football, baseball, cricket, golf, lacrosse, skateboarding, tennis, volleyball, walking, wrestling, and outdoor activities. Athletic footwear is primarily designed for specific athletic use, though a significant portion is worn casually. The Company emphasizes innovation and high-quality construction in product development and manufacturing. Sportswear, Running, and the Jordan Brand are currently the top-selling footwear categories and are expected to continue leading in footwear sales. Sports apparel, which features the same trademarks and is sold through similar marketing and distribution channels as footwear, is primarily designed for athletic use and is also focused on innovation and quality. Sportswear, Training, and Running are the top-selling apparel categories and are expected to lead in apparel sales. Footwear, apparel, and accessories are often marketed in “collections” by use or category, and apparel with licensed college and professional team and league logos is also sold. The Company sells performance equipment and accessories under the NIKE Brand, including bags, socks, sport balls, eyewear, timepieces, digital devices, bats, gloves, protective equipment, and other sports-related items. Small amounts of plastic products are sold to other manufacturers through its wholly-owned subsidiary, NIKE IHM, Inc., doing business as Air Manufacturing Innovation. The Jordan Brand designs, distributes, and licenses athletic and casual footwear, apparel, and accessories primarily focused on basketball using the Jumpman trademark, with sales and operating results reported within the respective NIKE Brand geographic operating segments. Converse, a wholly-owned subsidiary headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, designs, distributes, and licenses casual sneakers, apparel, and accessories under the Converse, Chuck Taylor, All Star, One Star, Star Chevron, and Jack Purcell trademarks, with operating results reported on a stand-alone basis. Hurley, a wholly-owned subsidiary headquartered in Costa Mesa, California, designs and distributes action sports and youth lifestyle apparel and accessories under the Hurley trademark, with sales and operating results included in the NIKE Brand’s North America geographic operating segment. In addition to direct sales to consumers and wholesale customers through NIKE Direct, the Company has license agreements allowing unaffiliated parties to manufacture and sell products using NIKE-owned trademarks, including apparel, digital devices, and applications. Sales and marketing experience moderate fluctuations in aggregate sales volume annually, with revenues in the first and fourth fiscal quarters historically slightly exceeding those in the second and third quarters. The mix of product sales varies due to seasonal and geographic demand, as well as macroeconomic, operating, and logistics factors. Consumer preferences, including trends in sports and fitness and design, influence demand, requiring the Company to adjust product mix, develop new products, and influence fitness trends through extensive marketing; failure to respond adequately could materially harm sales and profitability. The Company reports its NIKE Brand operations based on internal geographic segments: North America, Europe, Middle East & Africa (EMEA), Greater China, and Asia Pacific & Latin America (APLA), which include results for the NIKE, Jordan, and Hurley brands, with NIKE Direct sales managed within each segment. Converse is a separate reportable operating segment focused on the design, marketing, licensing, and sale of casual sneakers, apparel, and accessories, with direct-to-consumer operations, including digital commerce, reported within the Converse segment. In fiscal 2019, NIKE Brand and Converse sales in the United States accounted for approximately 41% of total revenues, compared to 42% and 46% in fiscal 2018 and 2017, respectively. The Company sells to thousands of retail accounts in the U.S., including footwear, sporting goods, athletic specialty, department, skate, tennis, and golf stores, and uses NIKE sales offices to solicit sales. During fiscal 2019, the three largest U.S. customers accounted for approximately 24% of U.S. sales. NIKE Direct and Converse direct-to-consumer operations sell products through various digital platforms and operate the following U.S. retail stores: 217 NIKE Brand factory stores, 29 NIKE Brand in-line stores (including employee-only), 109 Converse stores (including factory), and 29 Hurley stores (including factory and employee-only), totaling 384 stores. The Company has six significant distribution centers in the U.S.: four in Memphis, Tennessee (two owned, two leased), two in Indianapolis, Indiana, and Dayton, Tennessee (both leased and operated by third-party logistics providers), and one in Foothill Ranch, California (leased). Smaller leased and third-party operated distribution facilities are located in various parts of the U.S. For fiscal 2019, non-U.S. NIKE Brand and Converse sales accounted for approximately 59% of total revenues, compared to 58% and 54% in fiscal 2018 and 2017, respectively. Products are sold to retail accounts, through NIKE Direct, and via independent distributors, licensees, and sales representatives globally, with shipments from 67 distribution centers outside the U.S. During fiscal 2019, the three largest non-U.S. customers accounted for approximately 14% of total non-U.S. sales. NIKE Direct and Converse direct-to-consumer operations operate the following non-U.S. retail stores: 648 NIKE Brand factory stores, 57 NIKE Brand in-line stores (including employee-only), 63 Converse stores (including factory), totaling 768 stores. International branch offices and subsidiaries are located in Argentina, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bermuda, Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hong Kong, Hungary, India, Indonesia, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Korea, Macau, Malaysia, Mexico, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Panama, the Philippines, Poland, Portugal, Russia, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Sri Lanka, Sweden, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, Uruguay, and Vietnam. No customer accounted for 10% or more of worldwide net revenues during fiscal 2019. The Company believes research, design, and development are key to its success, with a focus on technical innovation in footwear, apparel, and equipment to enhance performance, reduce injury, maximize comfort, and minimize waste. The Company employs specialists in biomechanics, chemistry, exercise physiology, engineering, industrial design, sustainability, and related fields, and utilizes research committees and advisory boards composed of athletes, coaches, trainers, equipment managers, orthopedists, podiatrists, and other experts who review designs, materials, concepts, and manufacturing improvements and compliance with global safety regulations. Employee athletes, athletes under sports marketing contracts, and other athletes wear-test and evaluate products during development. As new technologies emerge, the Company integrates them into existing product categories based on market intelligence and consumer preferences. Examples include NIKE Air, Lunar, Zoom, Free, Flywire, Dri-Fit, Flyknit, Flyweave, ZoomX, React, Adaptive, and NIKE+ technologies, which are widely used across Running, NIKE Basketball, Jordan Brand, Football (Soccer), Training, and Sportswear. Manufacturing is conducted through 112 footwear factories located in 12 countries, with the largest single footwear factory being one of these.

Nike utilizes research committees and advisory boards composed of athletes, coaches, trainers, equipment managers, orthopedists, podiatrists, and other experts to review product designs, materials, concepts, manufacturing processes, and ensure compliance with global product safety regulations. Employee athletes, those under sports marketing contracts, and other athletes participate in wear-testing and evaluation of products during the design and development phase. As Nike develops new technologies, its design teams use market intelligence and research to identify opportunities to integrate innovations into existing product categories in response to consumer preferences. Technologies such as NIKE Air, Lunar, Zoom, Free, Flywire, Dri-Fit, Flyknit, Flyweave, ZoomX, React, Adaptive, and NIKE+ are widely incorporated across Running, NIKE Basketball, Jordan Brand, Football (Soccer), Training, and Sportswear categories. Nike is supplied by 112 footwear factories in 12 countries; the largest single factory accounted for about 9% of total fiscal 2019 footwear production. Virtually all footwear is manufactured outside the United States by independent contract manufacturers, with Vietnam, China, and Indonesia producing approximately 49%, 23%, and 21% of total footwear, respectively. Four contract manufacturers each accounted for over 10% of footwear production, collectively representing about 61% of total production. For apparel, Nike is supplied by 334 factories in 36 countries; the largest single apparel factory accounted for about 14% of total fiscal 2019 apparel production. China, Vietnam, and Thailand produced approximately 27%, 22%, and 10% of total apparel, respectively. One apparel contract manufacturer accounted for more than 10% of production, and the top five collectively accounted for about 49%. Principal footwear materials include natural and synthetic rubber, plastic compounds, foam cushioning, natural and synthetic leather, nylon, polyester, canvas, and polyurethane films used in NIKE Air-Sole components. Air Manufacturing Innovation, a wholly-owned subsidiary with facilities near Beaverton, Oregon and in St. Charles, Missouri, along with independent contractors in China and Vietnam, supplied Air-Sole cushioning in fiscal 2019. Apparel materials include natural and synthetic fabrics and threads (both virgin and recycled), specialized performance fabrics that wick moisture, retain heat, and repel rain or snow, and plastic and metal hardware. Raw materials are primarily sourced and purchased by independent contractors and suppliers in the countries where manufacturing occurs, and Nike’s contract manufacturers and suppliers have experienced little difficulty meeting raw material needs. Since 1972, Sojitz Corporation of America, a Japanese trading company and sole owner of Nike’s redeemable preferred stock, has provided import-export financing for Nike in markets including Argentina, Brazil, Canada, India, South Africa, and Uruguay, excluding products produced and sold in those countries. Approximately 5% of Nike Brand sales occurred in these countries. A failure by Sojitz America to provide these services or by its banks could disrupt product acquisition and delivery, leading to canceled orders and negative impacts on sales and profitability, though such disruptions would likely be short-term due to alternative financing options. International operations face risks such as changes in foreign and domestic trade policies, import duties, anti-dumping measures, quotas, safeguard measures, trade restrictions, fund transfer limitations, and political instability or terrorism, though Nike has not been materially affected and cannot predict future material impacts. Global economic and political uncertainty has increased protectionist actions, affecting many industries, including footwear and apparel, with companies like adidas, Anta, ASICS, Li Ning, lululemon athletica, Puma, Under Armour, and V.F. Corporation being key competitors. Nike is the world’s largest seller of athletic footwear and apparel, competing on product attributes such as quality, performance, innovation, price/value, consumer brand affinity, marketing, social media engagement, customer service, athlete endorsements, and effective sourcing and distribution. Nike believes it is competitive in all these areas. The company protects its intellectual property through trademarks, patents, and trade secrets, using trademarks on nearly all products, with NIKE and Swoosh Design being among its most valuable assets, registered in nearly 170 jurisdictions worldwide. Nike also holds common law rights in trade dress for significant shoe designs and has obtained trademark registrations for certain trade dress. It has copyright protection for original designs, graphics, and other works, and files, owns, and maintains U.S. and foreign utility and design patents covering components, technologies, materials, manufacturing techniques, features, functionality, and industrial and aesthetic designs. Nike’s success depends on its design, research and development, production, and marketing capabilities, supported by its intellectual property. The company applies for and registers intellectual property rights in the U.S. and select foreign countries for valuable trademarks, inventions, innovations, and designs and actively protects them against infringement. As of May 31, 2019, Nike had approximately 76,700 employees worldwide, including retail and part-time staff. No employees are unionized except in certain areas of the APLA geography, where local law requires union representation, and in some countries outside the U.S., where local laws require representation by works councils or similar organizations. In certain European countries, Nike is required to comply with industry-wide or national collective bargaining agreements. Nike has never experienced a material disruption of operations due to labor disputes. The executive officers of Nike, Inc. as of July 23, 2019, are Mark G. Parker, Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer, who joined in 1979 and has held key roles in product research, design, marketing, and brand management; Andrew Campion, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, who joined in 2007 and has led financial and strategic planning; Elliott Hill, President, Consumer and Marketplace, who joined in 1988 and has held various sales and retail leadership roles; Hilary K. Krane, Executive Vice President, Chief Administrative Officer, and General Counsel, who joined in 2010 and has held leadership roles in legal and corporate affairs; Monique S. Matheson, Executive Vice President, Global Human Resources, who joined in 1998 and has led human resources and talent development; and John F. Slusher, Executive Vice President, Global Sports Marketing, who joined in 1998 and has led global sports marketing. Eric D. Sprunk, Chief Operating Officer, joined in 1993 and has held various leadership roles in finance, operations, and merchandising, becoming Chief Operating Officer in 2013. NIKE’s products face intense competition both domestically and internationally, with competition from athletic and leisure footwear, apparel, and equipment companies, as well as diversified firms. NIKE also competes for production capacity from independent manufacturers and faces competition from multi-brand retailers through its NIKE Direct operations, including digital commerce and retail stores. Product offerings, technologies, marketing expenditures, pricing, production costs, customer service, digital platforms, and social media presence are key competitive areas. Rapid changes in technology and consumer preferences add significant risk. Retail competition, including shifts in consumer shopping habits and the rise of digital commerce, also pose risks to both NIKE Direct and wholesale operations. Failure to anticipate and respond to competitors’ actions could lead to increased costs or declining consumer demand. Maintaining brand image and reputation is critical, as success depends on design, marketing, product innovation, and quality. The ability to adapt to a changing media environment, including social media and digital advertising, is essential. Negative claims or publicity involving NIKE, its products, consumer data, or key employees, endorsers, or suppliers—regardless of accuracy—could damage the brand. Social media can amplify negative publicity, making responses more challenging. Adverse publicity related to regulatory or legal actions could harm consumer confidence and reduce long-term demand. If brand reputation is tarnished or negative publicity arises, sales, financial condition, and operating results could be materially and adversely affected. NIKE’s success depends on its ability to identify and respond to changing consumer preferences and product trends. However, lead times for products may hinder rapid response to trends. Consumer preferences can shift quickly, and if NIKE fails to adjust product mix, develop new products, or influence fitness trends through marketing, it could face lower sales, excess inventory, or reduced profit margins. Global marketing efforts through social media, mobile apps, and online advertising are essential, and failure to market effectively or rising advertising costs could harm the business. Technical innovation and quality control in product design and manufacturing are essential for commercial success. NIKE relies on specialists in biomechanics, chemistry, exercise physiology, engineering, industrial design, sustainability, and expert advisory boards—including athletes, coaches, orthopedists, and podiatrists—to develop and test performance products. If innovation is lacking or product quality issues arise, consumer demand could decline, and significant remediation costs could result. Maintaining relationships with professional athletes, sports teams, leagues, and public figures is vital for product authenticity and brand visibility. However, as competition increases, the cost of securing and retaining these relationships has risen. If NIKE cannot maintain these associations or do so at reasonable cost, it may lose visibility or authenticity and be forced to increase marketing spending. If endorsers stop using products contrary to agreements or take actions that harm their own reputations, it could damage NIKE’s brand and sales. Poor performance by endorsers, failure to identify promising athletes or organizations, or inability to secure cost-effective endorsement deals could also harm brand value, sales, and profitability. General economic factors, including inflation and currency exchange rate fluctuations, affect revenues, costs, and margins. A majority of NIKE’s products are manufactured and sold outside the United States, and transactions occur in various currencies, increasing exposure to global economic volatility, including Brexit and U.S. policy changes affecting the U.S. Dollar. Currency fluctuations can reduce the U.S. Dollar value of foreign sales and earnings and increase costs for independent manufacturers. NIKE hedges certain foreign currency exposures to mitigate, but not eliminate, the impact of exchange rate fluctuations. These hedges reduce both the negative and positive effects of currency movements, and future financial results are significantly influenced by the value of the U.S. Dollar relative to foreign currencies. The degree of impact depends on hedging activities. Global economic conditions, especially in emerging markets, can adversely affect business operations. Slower consumer spending may reduce demand, lead to lower orders, cancellations, higher discounts, increased inventory, and lower gross margins. Access to financing in credit and capital markets may become difficult, affecting NIKE’s ability to fund operations. Volatility in foreign exchange rates and commodity prices—such as cotton or petroleum derivatives—can increase costs and reduce profitability. If retailers face financial difficulties or struggle to obtain financing, they may cancel orders, delay payments, or fail to invest in merchandising, reducing sales and orders. Retailer insolvency could negatively impact product sales. If contract manufacturers or supply chain participants face financing challenges, shipments may be delayed or not delivered. NIKE’s business is affected by seasonality, with revenues in the first and fourth fiscal quarters historically slightly exceeding those in the second and third quarters. Sales volume fluctuates due to seasonal and geographic demand, timing of major sporting events like the NBA Finals, Olympics, or World Cup, and changes in order mix or delivery schedules. Customers may cancel orders or change delivery timelines with minimal notice, making accurate quarterly sales forecasting difficult. As a result, operating results are likely to fluctuate significantly from period to period. Seasonality, combined with other uncontrollable factors such as economic conditions, consumer preferences, weather, import quotas, transportation disruptions, and currency fluctuations, can adversely affect business performance. Operating margins are also sensitive to manufacturing and transportation costs, shifts in product mix, and geographic sales trends. Results from any period should not be viewed as indicative of future performance. NIKE extends credit to customers based on financial condition without requiring collateral and offers advance orders up to six months in advance under a futures ordering program. These orders may be canceled, especially with financially unstable retailers or those facing economic uncertainty. Past customer bankruptcies have negatively impacted sales, receivables collection, and financial condition. A weakening retail economy or shifts in consumer behavior may lead retailers to be more cautious with orders. Slowing or changing economic conditions in key markets could harm customer financial health, affecting NIKE’s results. Product sales also depend on high-quality merchandising and appealing retail environments, which require ongoing retailer investment. If retailers face financial difficulties, they may delay or forgo such investments, leading to lower sales and orders. Failure to accurately forecast consumer demand could result in excess inventory or shortages, leading to reduced operating margins, lower cash flows, and harm to the business.

Customers are encouraged to place orders for products five to six months before delivery through the company’s futures ordering program. These advance orders can be canceled under specific conditions, and the risk of cancellation increases when dealing with financially unstable retailers or those facing economic uncertainty. In the past, some customers have encountered financial difficulties, including bankruptcies, which have negatively impacted sales, the company’s ability to collect receivables, and its financial condition. When the retail economy weakens or consumer behavior shifts, retailers may become more cautious in placing orders. A slowdown or change in the economy in key markets could harm the financial health of customers, thereby adversely affecting the company’s results of operations and financial condition. Product sales depend partly on high-quality merchandising and an appealing retail environment, which requires ongoing investments by retailers. If retailers face financial difficulties, they may fail to make or delay such investments, leading to lower sales and reduced orders. Inaccurate forecasting of consumer demand can result in excess inventories or shortages, which may reduce operating margins, harm cash flows, and negatively impact the business. To meet anticipated demand, the company purchases products from manufacturers outside the futures program and in advance of customer orders, holding them in inventory to resell. There is a risk that excess products may not be sold, leading to inventory write-downs or discounted sales that could damage brand image and harm operating results, financial condition, and cash flows. Conversely, underestimating demand or failing to receive required products from manufacturers on time may cause inventory shortages, delaying shipments, damaging relationships with retailers, distributors, and consumers, and reducing brand loyalty. The difficulty in forecasting demand also makes it challenging to predict future results of operations, financial condition, and cash flows. A failure to accurately predict demand could adversely affect net revenues and net income, and such effects cannot be reliably forecast in advance. Consolidation among retailers or concentration of market share among a few large retailers increases the company’s credit risk and limits its ability to sell products. In some countries, a few large athletic footwear, apparel, and equipment retailers dominate the market, often expanding through acquisitions or store construction. This concentration increases credit risk, and if any of these retailers face liquidity issues or a shift in consumer behavior away from traditional retail, their outstanding payables may not be paid. Increased market share concentration among a few retailers in a region means that if one significantly reduces purchases, the company may not find enough alternative retail outlets to maintain sales and revenues. The company’s NIKE Direct operations require substantial investment in equipment, leasehold improvements, information systems, and personnel, with significant operating lease commitments. Some stores are designed as high-profile venues for brand promotion, requiring greater investment due to unique design, location, and size. Due to high fixed costs, declines in sales, shifts in consumer behavior away from brick-and-mortar retail, or poor performance of individual or multiple stores could lead to significant lease termination costs, write-offs of equipment and leasehold improvements, and employee-related expenses. Retail operations face various risks, including credit card fraud, mismanagement of retail partners, and cost challenges in store construction and operation. Extreme weather in store locations could also harm the business. If the technology systems enabling online shopping do not function effectively, the company’s operating results and global growth in digital commerce could be materially harmed. Many consumers shop through digital platforms, increasingly using mobile devices and apps for online shopping and comparison. The company uses social media and proprietary mobile apps to engage consumers and enhance the shopping experience. Failure to provide effective, reliable, user-friendly digital platforms with a wide product selection and fast delivery could result in a competitive disadvantage, loss of digital sales, reputational harm, and negative impacts on digital commerce growth and overall business performance. Risks specific to digital commerce include sales diversion from brick-and-mortar stores, difficulty replicating the in-store experience online, and liability for online content. Failure to address these risks could harm digital sales and damage brand reputation. Inadequate protection or enforcement of intellectual property rights could harm the business. The company periodically discovers counterfeit or infringing products; if enforcement fails, continued sales of such products could reduce sales, damage the brand, and shift consumer preference. Efforts to protect intellectual property may not prevent imitation, and third parties may block sales as violations of proprietary rights. The company may face liability if third parties claim infringement, which could be costly and time-consuming, requiring expensive license agreements or resulting in significant damages or injunctions. The company takes measures to prevent unauthorized use or disclosure of confidential information, including non-disclosure and non-compete agreements, collaboration agreements, and training. However, these controls may not be effective, and sensitive information such as business strategy, new technologies, financial results, or personal data could be improperly used or disclosed, leading to reputational damage, stock price declines, market position loss, and legal penalties. In some countries, intellectual property laws do not offer the same level of protection as U.S. laws, increasing costs and liability in protecting rights, both domestically and internationally. Failure to protect intellectual property or resolve conflicts could harm the business or financial condition. The company faces data security and privacy risks due to handling customer and user data, including transactional and personal information. Sophisticated hackers and data thieves use social engineering and large-scale automated attacks that can go undetected for long periods. A breach of the company’s or its service providers’ systems could result in loss of confidential data, misuse of personal information, business disruption, unwanted media attention, damaged consumer relationships, reputational harm, lost sales, legal actions, and significant remediation expenses. Compliance with complex and evolving data privacy regulations, such as the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which became effective on May 25, 2018, and California’s Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), effective in 2020, imposes additional obligations and individual rights, increasing compliance costs. Failure to comply could lead to legal and reputational risks, misuse of personal data, government proceedings, reputational damage, and reduced revenues and profits. The company is exposed to risks if licensees fail to generate expected sales or maintain brand value. It licenses trademarks and copyrighted material to third parties; if licensees fail to market or sell products, lack capital, or mismanage operations, customer relationships, labor, or credit risks, revenues could decline both directly through reduced royalties and indirectly through lower sales of other products. The company relies on licensees to preserve brand value, but cannot fully control how brands are used. Misuse or negative publicity involving a licensee could harm the brand and the company. Contractors or licensees’ contractors may fail to comply with the company’s code of conduct or local laws and environmental, health, and safety standards, which could harm the business. The company works with hundreds of foreign contractors to manufacture products and allows unaffiliated parties to manufacture using its intellectual property. Contractors must comply with a code of conduct and product safety standards; however, noncompliance with these standards or local laws, or failure by licensees to enforce them, could damage the company’s reputation, lead to product recalls, and negatively affect sales and financial condition. Negative publicity about production methods or workplace conditions could harm brand image and force the company to seek alternative suppliers or licenses. International operations carry inherent risks, including foreign laws, varying consumer preferences, political unrest, shipment disruptions, and economic changes in manufacturing or sales countries. This includes uncertainty from Brexit, changes in U.S. and international tax laws and trade policies, and the U.S. administration’s focus on discouraging outsourcing through tariffs or penalties, which may require business changes and harm results. Disease outbreaks, terrorist acts, and military conflict also increase risks to manufacturing, importing, selling, and operating costs. If any of these factors make business in a country impractical, the company’s operations could be harmed. Many imported products face duties, tariffs, or quotas that affect cost and volume. Countries may eliminate, adjust, or impose new quotas, duties, tariffs, safeguard measures, anti-dumping duties, cargo restrictions, currency transfer limits, climate change legislation, or product safety regulations, all of which could negatively affect operations and financial condition. The company is subject to changes in tax rates, new tax laws, additional liabilities, or increased volatility in its effective tax rate. It operates under U.S. and foreign tax laws, with significant changes introduced by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Tax Act) on December 22, 2017, including a one-time transition tax on foreign earnings, a corporate tax rate reduction from 35% to 21%, and a shift from a worldwide to a modified territorial tax system with base erosion measures affecting foreign earnings. Implementation of the Tax Act led to increased tax expense and effective tax rate in fiscal 2018; the company completed its analysis in the second quarter of fiscal 2019 with no adjustments. A substantial portion of income is earned abroad, and proposals to reform foreign tax laws could significantly impact U.S. multinational taxation on foreign earnings. Although the outcome is uncertain, such proposals, if enacted, could harm income tax expense and cash flows. Portions of operations benefit from reduced or zero tax rates under tax holidays or rulings, which may expire or be terminated based on conditions. For example, in January 2019, the European Commission opened an investigation into whether the Netherlands breached State Aid rules by granting tax rulings to the company. If the investigation is adversely resolved, the Netherlands may assess additional taxes, increasing future income taxes. The company is also subject to audits by the U.S. Internal Revenue Service and other tax authorities. It regularly assesses the likelihood of adverse outcomes to determine tax provision adequacy. Although it believes its provisions are sufficient, final audit results or disputes could materially differ from historical accruals, negatively affecting financial statements. For instance, intercompany transactions across tax jurisdictions may be challenged by tax authorities, resulting in adjustments that alter earnings distribution across countries with different tax rates. Changes in U.S. or international trade policies, including renegotiation or termination of trade agreements, imposition of higher tariffs, economic sanctions, or other regulations affecting trade with key markets, could adversely affect the company’s reputation, business, financial condition, and results of operations.

NIKE, Inc. engages in numerous intercompany transactions across multiple tax jurisdictions, and although it believes these transactions accurately reflect their economic realities and has proper local transfer pricing documentation in place, tax authorities may propose and sustain adjustments that could alter the company’s earnings mix across countries with different statutory tax rates. Changes in U.S. trade policy, including tariff and import/export regulations, or failure to comply with such regulations, could materially harm the company’s reputation, business, financial condition, and results of operations. Shifts in U.S. or international social, political, regulatory, or economic conditions—such as changes in foreign trade, manufacturing, development, or investment laws—along with negative sentiment toward the U.S., could adversely affect the company’s business. The U.S. presidential administration has implemented or proposed changes to trade policies, including renegotiating or terminating trade agreements, imposing higher tariffs on imports, and enforcing economic sanctions on individuals, corporations, or countries, which may be time-consuming and costly to comply with. These policy changes may lead to greater restrictions and economic disincentives in international trade, with retaliatory actions by foreign governments, such as imposing tariffs on U.S. goods, potentially disrupting global trade. As a multinational corporation, NIKE conducts significant business affected by U.S. and foreign trade policies, including tariffs, trade agreements, and sanctions, which could negatively impact the U.S. economy, specific sectors, the company’s industry, and global demand for its products, thereby harming its business, financial condition, and results of operations. If one or more of NIKE’s counterparty financial institutions default on their obligations or fail, the company could incur significant losses. DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS  
NIKE, Inc. is a worldwide leader in the design, development and worldwide marketing and selling of athletic footwear, apparel, equipment, accessories and services. NIKE, Inc. portfolio brands include the NIKE Brand, Jordan Brand, Hurley and Converse. The NIKE Brand is focused on performance athletic footwear, apparel, equipment, accessories and services across a wide range of sport categories, amplified with sport-inspired sportswear products carrying the Swoosh trademark, as well as other NIKE Brand trademarks. The Jordan Brand is focused on athletic and casual footwear, apparel and accessories using the Jumpman trademark. Sales and operating results of Jordan Brand products are reported within the respective NIKE Brand geographic operating segments. The Hurley brand is focused on action sports and youth lifestyle apparel and accessories under the Hurley trademark. Sales and operating results of Hurley brand products are reported within the NIKE Brand's North America geographic operating segment. Converse designs, distributes, licenses and sells casual sneakers, apparel and accessories under the Converse, Chuck Taylor, All Star, One Star, Star Chevron and Jack Purcell trademarks. In some markets outside the U.S., these trademarks are licensed to third parties who design, distribute, market and sell similar products. Operating results of the Converse brand are reported on a stand-alone basis.  
BASIS OF CONSOLIDATION  
The Consolidated Financial Statements include the accounts of NIKE, Inc. and its subsidiaries (the "Company" or "NIKE"). All significant intercompany transactions and balances have been eliminated.  
REVENUE RECOGNITION  
Beginning in fiscal 2019, the Company adopted Accounting Standards Update (ASU) No. 2014-09, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (Topic 606). Prior period amounts have not been restated and continue to be reported in accordance with the Company's historical accounting policies. The Company's revenue recognition policies under Topic 606 are described in the following paragraphs and references to prior period policies under Accounting Standard Codification Topic 605 — Revenue Recognition (Topic 605), are included below in the event they are substantially different.  
Revenue transactions associated with the sale of NIKE Brand footwear, apparel and equipment, as well as Converse products, comprise a single performance obligation, which consists of the sale of products to customers either through wholesale or direct to consumer channels. The Company satisfies the performance obligation and records revenues when transfer of control has passed to the customer, based on the terms of sale. A customer is considered to have control once they are able to direct the use and receive substantially all of the benefits of the product.  
Transfer of control passes to wholesale customers upon shipment or upon receipt depending on the country of the sale and the agreement with the customer. Control passes to retail store customers at the time of sale and to substantially all digital commerce customers upon shipment. Prior to June 1, 2018, the requirements for recognizing revenue were met upon delivery to the customer. The transaction price is determined based upon the invoiced sales price, less anticipated sales returns, discounts and miscellaneous claims from customers. Payment terms for wholesale transactions depend on the country of sale or agreement with the customer and payment is generally required within 90 days or less of shipment to or receipt by the wholesale customer. Payment is due at the time of sale for retail store and digital commerce transactions.  
Consideration for trademark licensing contracts is earned through sales-based or usage-based royalty arrangements and the associated revenues are recognized over the license period.  
Taxes assessed by governmental authorities that are both imposed on and concurrent with a specific revenue-producing transaction, and are collected by the Company from a customer, are excluded from Revenues and Cost of sales in the Consolidated Statements of Income. Shipping and handling costs associated with outbound freight after control over a product has transferred to a customer are accounted for as a fulfillment cost and are included in Cost of sales when the related revenue is recognized.  
SALES-RELATED RESERVES  
Consideration promised in the Company's contracts with customers is variable due to anticipated reductions such as sales returns, discounts and miscellaneous claims from customers. The Company estimates the most likely amount it will be entitled to receive and records an anticipated reduction against Revenues, with an offsetting increase to Accrued liabilities at the time revenues are recognized. The estimated cost of inventory for product returns is recorded in Prepaid expenses and other current assets on the Consolidated Balance Sheets. Prior to June 1, 2018, the Company's reserve balances were reported net of the estimated cost of inventory for product returns and recognized within Accounts receivable, net for wholesale transactions and Accrued liabilities for the Company's direct to consumer business, on the Consolidated Balance Sheets.  
The provision for anticipated sales returns consists of both contractual return rights and discretionary authorized returns. Provisions for post-invoice sales discounts consist of both contractual programs and discretionary discounts that are expected to be granted at a later date.  
Estimates of discretionary authorized returns, discounts and claims are based on (1) historical rates, (2) specific identification of outstanding returns not yet received from customers and outstanding discounts and claims and (3) estimated returns, discounts and claims expected, but not yet finalized with customers. Actual returns, discounts and claims in any future period are inherently uncertain and thus may differ from estimates recorded. If actual or expected future returns, discounts or claims were significantly greater or lower than the reserves established, a reduction or increase to net revenues would be recorded in the period in which such determination was made.  
COST OF SALES  
Cost of sales consists primarily of inventory costs, as well as warehousing costs (including the cost of warehouse labor), third-party royalties, certain foreign currency hedge gains and losses and product design costs. Shipping and handling costs are expensed as incurred and included in Cost of sales.  
DEMAND CREATION EXPENSE  
Demand creation expense consists of advertising and promotion costs, including costs of endorsement contracts, complimentary product, television, digital and print advertising and media costs, brand events and retail brand presentation. Advertising production costs are expensed the first time an advertisement is run. Advertising media costs are expensed when the advertisement appears. Costs related to brand events are expensed when the event occurs. Costs related to retail brand presentation are expensed when the presentation is complete and delivered.  
A significant amount of the Company's promotional expenses result from payments under endorsement contracts. In general, endorsement payments are expensed on a straight-line basis over the term of the contract. However, certain contract elements may be accounted for differently based upon the facts and circumstances of each individual contract. Prepayments made under contracts are included in Prepaid expenses and other current assets or Deferred income taxes and other assets depending on the period to which the prepayment applies.  
Certain contracts provide for contingent payments to endorsers based upon specific achievements in their sport (e.g., winning a championship). The Company records Demand creation expense for these amounts when the endorser achieves the specific goal.  
Certain contracts provide for variable payments based upon endorsers maintaining a level of performance in their sport over an extended period of time (e.g., maintaining a specified ranking in a sport for a year). When the Company determines payments are probable, the amounts are reported in Demand creation expense ratably over the contract period based on the Company's best estimate of the endorser's performance. In these instances, to the extent actual payments to the endorser differ from the Company's estimate due to changes in the endorser's performance, adjustments to Demand creation expense may be recorded in a future period.  
Certain contracts provide for royalty payments to endorsers based upon a predetermined percent of sales of particular products, which the Company records in Cost of sales as the related sales occur. For contracts containing minimum guaranteed royalty payments, the Company records the amount of any guaranteed payment in excess of that earned through sales of product within Demand creation expense.  
Through cooperative advertising programs, the Company reimburses its wholesale customers for certain costs of advertising the Company's products. The Company records these costs in Demand creation expense at the point in time when it is obligated to its customers for the costs. This obligation may arise prior to the related advertisement being run.

Operating overhead expense consists primarily of wage and benefit-related expenses, research and development costs, as well as other administrative expenses, such as rent, depreciation and amortization, professional services, meetings and travel.

SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT COSTS  
Internal Use Software: Expenditures for major software purchases and software developed for internal use are capitalized and amortized over a 2 to 12-year period on a straight-line basis. The Company's policy provides for the capitalization of external direct costs associated with developing or obtaining internal use computer software. In addition, the Company also capitalizes certain payroll and payroll-related costs for employees who are directly associated with internal use computer software projects. The amount of capitalizable payroll costs with respect to these employees is limited to the time directly spent on such projects. Costs associated with preliminary project stage activities, training, maintenance and all other post-implementation stage activities are expensed as incurred.  
Computer Software to be Sold, Leased or Otherwise Marketed: Development costs of computer software to be sold, leased or otherwise marketed as an integral part of a product are subject to capitalization beginning when a product's technological feasibility has been established and ending when a product is available for general release to customers. In most instances, the Company's products are released soon after technological feasibility has been established. Therefore, software development costs incurred subsequent to achievement of technological feasibility are usually not significant, and generally most software development costs have been expensed as incurred.  
IMPAIRMENT OF LONG-LIVED ASSETS  
The Company reviews the carrying value of long-lived assets or asset groups to be used in operations whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying amount of the assets might not be recoverable. Factors that would necessitate an impairment assessment include a significant adverse change in the extent or manner in which an asset is used, a significant adverse change in legal factors or the business climate that could affect the value of the asset or a significant decline in the observable market value of an asset, among others. If such facts indicate a potential impairment, the Company would assess the recoverability of an asset group by determining if the carrying value of the asset group exceeds the sum of the projected undiscounted cash flows expected to result from the use and eventual disposition of the assets over the remaining economic life of the primary asset in the asset group. If the recoverability test indicates that the carrying value of the asset group is not recoverable, the Company will estimate the fair value of the asset group using appropriate valuation methodologies, which would typically include an estimate of discounted cash flows. Any impairment would be measured as the difference between the asset group's carrying amount and its estimated fair value.  
GOODWILL AND INDEFINITE-LIVED INTANGIBLE ASSETS  
The Company performs annual impairment tests on goodwill and intangible assets with indefinite lives in the fourth quarter of each fiscal year or when events occur or circumstances change that would, more likely than not, reduce the fair value of a reporting unit or an intangible asset with an indefinite life below its carrying value. Events or changes in circumstances that may trigger interim impairment reviews include significant changes in business climate, operating results, planned investments in the reporting unit, planned divestitures or an expectation that the carrying amount may not be recoverable, among other factors. The Company may first assess qualitative factors to determine whether it is more likely than not that the fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying amount. If, after assessing the totality of events and circumstances, the Company determines it is more likely than not that the fair value of the reporting unit is greater than its carrying amount, an impairment test is unnecessary. If an impairment test is necessary, the Company will estimate the fair value of its related reporting units. If the carrying value of a reporting unit exceeds its fair value, the goodwill of that reporting unit is determined to be impaired and the Company will proceed with recording an impairment charge equal to the excess of the carrying value over the related fair value.

The Preferred Stock may also be redeemed at $1.00 per share plus accrued dividends and interest under other circumstances. When the number of outstanding shares of Class B Common Stock is 25% or more of total Common Stock, Class A and Class B Common Stock holders vote separately for director elections, with Class B holders electing 25% (rounded up) of the authorized directors. If Class A Common Stock is less than 12.5% of total Common Stock, Class B holders still elect 25% of directors, and the remainder are elected by all Common Stock holders voting together. If Class B Common Stock is less than 25% of total Common Stock, all Common Stock holders vote together to elect directors. Dividends on Preferred Stock are preferential and cumulative at $0.10 per share per annum, with unpaid dividends accruing interest at 12% per annum. Common Stock holders are entitled to share ratably in dividends when declared by the Board of Directors, but dividends on Common Stock may not be paid unless all Preferred Stock dividends for the fiscal year have been declared and paid or set apart. In liquidation or dissolution, holders of Preferred Stock are entitled to receive $1.00 per share plus unpaid dividends before any distribution to Common Stock holders. Certain provisions in the Articles of Incorporation and By-Laws have anti-takeover effects, including a requirement that 80% of outstanding Common Stock, voting together as one class, must approve a merger, sale of assets, or similar transaction with a beneficial holder of 10% or more of Common Stock, unless approved by the Board of Directors, and such vote must include at least 50% of the Common Stock held by non-interested parties. Any amendment to the 80% voting requirements, the number of directors, or director removal also requires 80% approval of outstanding Common Stock. These provisions may make it difficult for a shareholder or group owning more than 20% of Common Stock to effect a merger or acquisition, potentially preventing a majority of voting Common Stock holders from achieving required shareholder approval.
